title: Building a content loop that starts in operations
dek: How SIndustries turns daily ops notes into a weekly content review, a Tasks API content task, and a published website entry — without anyone manually translating signal into copy.
body:
Most company websites are updated in bursts. Someone remembers to write a blog post. Someone else remembers to file a release note. The result is content that lags reality by weeks, and a publishing muscle that only fires when the founder has the time and energy.

SIndustries is building a different loop. Operating signal — what shipped, what changed, what was decided — is captured as it happens, distilled on a fixed cadence, and routed into the website through a workflow with explicit review and approval boundaries. The loop runs whether or not anyone has the time that week.

## Where the signal starts

The loop begins in two places: agent heartbeats and Tom's chat context. Both feed structured rows into daily ops notes at brain/ops/notes/YYYY-MM-DD.md. Each row names the system or experiment, describes what happened, explains why it is content-relevant, and links to a reference file. Heartbeat appends the rows; nothing is interpreted at the time of capture.

This is deliberate. Capture is cheap; classification is expensive. The notes file becomes a time-stamped ledger of what the studio actually did, not what someone thinks it should have done.

## From notes to review

Once a week, a cron reads the last seven days of notes and distils them into a single review file at brain/content/sindustries-weekly-content/YYYY-MM-DD.md. The distil step is the only LLM-driven step in the pipeline; the output is structured by the review template (factual items, narrative items, deferred items) and explicitly separates changes that a delegated approver can ship from changes that need the founder's voice.

The review file is then promoted into a Tasks API content task. The task body contains the review file link, the review window, and the change items split into the two approval buckets. From that point the loop is mechanical: the Lobster validates format, gates on Ivy's capacity, and assigns the task for authoring.

## From task to website

Ivy is the content agent. She reads the source review, applies the content-authoring skill, and produces the JSON file changes that match the task's acceptance criteria. For factual items — release entries, status updates, metadata bumps, proof rewrites — the work lands on a Quinn-approval PR. For narrative items — new systems, new stories, first-person copy — the work lands on a Tom-approval PR.

Splitting the PRs by approval risk is the part that makes the loop sustainable. The founder's review time is reserved for the things that actually need a founder. The delegated approver handles everything that does not. Both PRs are authored by Ivy so review comments land on the same branch that produced the draft.

## Why the loop exists

The point of the loop is not to publish more. It is to publish what already happened, on a cadence that does not depend on anyone remembering to do it. The studio's working memory becomes the website's working memory. Drift between operating reality and public signal stops being a thing that has to be fixed in arrears.
